description: Test your knowledge of PA H11 | Plasma Cell Dyscrasias (Multiple Myeloma).

cards.text: Define multiple myeloma and explain why it is called 'clonal'.
cards.answer: Multiple myeloma is a malignant neoplasm of clonal plasma cells proliferating in bone marrow and secreting a single monoclonal protein (M-protein). Clonal means all malignant cells descend from one transformed precursor and produce identical immunoglobulin.

tip.tip: One abnormal cell → identical clones → one useless M-protein

cards.text: What does CRAB stand for in multiple myeloma, and how does each component occur?
cards.answer: C=Hypercalcaemia (osteoclastic resorption), R=Renal failure (light chain cast nephropathy, amyloidosis), A=Anaemia (marrow replacement, chronic disease cytokines), B=Bone lytic lesions (RANKL-driven osteoclast activation, DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts).

tip.tip: CRAB = the 4 myeloma-defining organ damage events

cards.text: What is immune paresis in MM and what is its clinical consequence?
cards.answer: Immune paresis is suppression of normal immunoglobulin production by non-malignant plasma cells. Result: recurrent infections from lack of protective antibodies and neutropenia; encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus) predominate.

tip.tip: Tumor makes useless M-protein → normal Ig suppressed → infections

cards.text: Explain the role of IL-6 in MM pathogenesis.
cards.answer: IL-6 is the principal growth and survival factor for myeloma cells, produced by stromal cells and myeloma cells in an autocrine/paracrine loop. It drives clonal expansion and resistance to apoptosis.

tip.tip: IL-6 = myeloma's favourite cytokine; stromal cells feed the tumor

cards.text: Describe the characteristic bone lesions in MM and contrast with other bone diseases.
cards.answer: 'Punched-out' lytic (osteolytic) lesions with no sclerotic rim on X-ray, predilecting in axial skeleton. Pure osteolytic pattern differs from metastatic carcinoma (often osteoblastic) and Paget's disease (both osteoclasts and osteoblasts increased).

tip.tip: MM = purely destructive; no new bone formation

cards.text: What is Bence-Jones protein and how does it cause renal damage?
cards.answer: Bence-Jones protein is free light chains (κ or λ) spilled into urine from M-protein production. Causes cast nephropathy ('myeloma kidney') by precipitation with Tamm-Horsfall protein in tubules, forming obstructive casts → tubular atrophy and renal failure.

tip.tip: Light chains + Tamm-Horsfall = blocked kidney tubules

cards.text: Which immunoglobulin types comprise the M-protein in MM? What is the rank order?
cards.answer: IgG (most common, ~70%) > IgA > IgD > IgM/IgE (rare). The monoclonal protein is functionally useless yet accumulates to high concentrations and suppresses normal Ig production.

tip.tip: IgG > IgA > IgD > IgM/IgE in frequency

cards.text: Explain the osteoclast-osteoblast imbalance in MM bone disease via RANKL and DKK-1.
cards.answer: Myeloma cells and stromal cells produce RANK-L, which activates osteoclasts. Simultaneously, myeloma cells produce DKK-1, which suppresses osteoblasts. Net result: unopposed osteoclastic resorption with no new bone formation.

tip.tip: RANKL ON osteoclasts + DKK-1 OFF osteoblasts = pure bone destruction
